program_overview.title: Reasoning and Readiness for Young Thinkers (Ages 6 to 9)
program_overview.tagline: Patterns, shapes, folding, sorting and number play: the thinking that ability screenings look for, built through puzzles, never through test-item drilling.
program_overview.description:
Many schools and districts look for advanced learners in the early grades, and some use group ability tests to help. These tests are designed to measure reasoning, not school knowledge. Riverside Insights, the publisher of the Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT), explains it this way: "Unlike a traditional achievement test, which measures how well a student has mastered the curriculum, the Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT) shows us how well a child can reason abstractly and identify patterns and relationships in the world around them." CogAT measures reasoning in three batteries, Verbal, Quantitative and Nonverbal, and at the levels for grades K to 2 its items are picture based. Pearson describes the Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test, Third Edition (NNAT3) as "a nonverbal measure of general ability for students in kindergarten through grade 12", and says the Otis-Lennon School Ability Test, Eighth Edition (OLSAT 8) "assesses verbal, nonverbal, and quantitative cognitive abilities for K-12 students".

Because these tests aim to measure reasoning, honest preparation looks different from cramming. Seattle Public Schools, for example, answers the question "Does my child need to study for the NGAT?" (the Naglieri General Ability Test it uses for first graders) with: "No. The NGAT is not designed to measure skills that can be learned through studying or test preparation." The process NYC Public Schools describes for Gifted and Talented entry in fall 2027 includes no admissions test: kindergarten eligibility comes from pre-K teacher nominations or Division of Early Childhood Education interviews, and for grades 1 to 4 NYC Public Schools looks at report card grades of 3 or 4 in Math, Reading and Writing.

So this course is not test prep in the drilling sense. It is a warm, playful reasoning class for children aged 6 to 9 that grows the broad skills such screenings look for: seeing patterns, comparing and classifying, picturing shapes turning and folding, and understanding numbers deeply. Every puzzle is our own, made for this course, and none is presented as a real test item. Near the end, children meet the general shape of a group test (listening to directions, choosing from options, working quietly for a set time) so that a screening day feels familiar rather than strange. Families in the UK whose child has been noticed as more able at school can use the same course for enrichment. We are independent of Riverside Insights, Pearson and every school district, and we make no promise about any screening result or program place.
what_makes_this_different: Reasoning taught through play: pattern blocks, folding paper, sorting games and number puzzles, never worksheets of imitation test items
All four kinds of thinking covered: pattern, spatial, verbal-free figural reasoning and quantitative reasoning
Number sense built properly alongside, so quantitative reasoning rests on real understanding
Honest about screening tests, quoting what the publishers and districts say they measure
Gentle familiarity with the format of a group test near the end, so a screening day is not a shock
Short, lively classes for ages 6 to 7 and 8 to 9, with a few minutes of puzzle play at home

learning_path.phase_1: Seeing patterns and sorting: repeating and growing patterns, odd one out, alike and different, and the first number patterns
learning_path.phase_2: Spatial and quantitative reasoning: turning, flipping and folding shapes, matrices of pictures and shapes, number sense, balance puzzles and number series
learning_path.phase_3: Putting it together: multi-step puzzles, explaining your thinking, and calm familiarity with how a group screening works

career_outcomes: Spotting the rule behind a pattern and explaining it in words
Picturing shapes as they turn, flip and fold
Comparing and classifying pictures, shapes and numbers by more than one feature
Strong number sense: place value, number bonds, comparing and estimating
Patience with puzzles that do not give up their answer at once
Confidence to sit quietly, listen to instructions and do their best on a new kind of task

phase_1_patterns_and_sorting.title: PHASE 1: Seeing Patterns and Sorting (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_patterns_and_sorting.description: The first habits of reasoning: noticing what repeats, what changes and what belongs together.

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Repeating Patterns and What Comes Next
topics: Repeating patterns of colors, shapes and sizes with real objects
Finding the part that repeats and saying it aloud
What comes next, and what is missing from the middle
Making your own pattern for a friend to continue
Patterns with two changes at once: color and size
A gentle starting puzzle set of our own to see where each child is
projects: A pattern necklace or pattern strip the child designs and explains
week_1_2.practice: Five minutes a day of pattern spotting at home, with our printable puzzle cards

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Growing Patterns and Shape Changes
topics: Growing patterns: towers that get taller by the same amount
Shapes that rotate a little each step
Shapes that gain a part each step
Patterns in grids: rows and columns that follow a rule
Describing a rule in a full sentence
Checking a guess against every step, not just the last one
projects: Build a growing pattern with blocks and draw the next two steps
week_3_4.practice: Original grid puzzles, from easy to stretching
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 puzzle check: a friendly set of our own pattern puzzles, talked through with the teacher

month_2_sorting_and_classifying.title: Month 2: Alike, Different and Belonging Together

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Sorting and Classifying
topics: Sorting objects by one feature, then by two
Odd one out, and explaining why
Which picture belongs with this group, and what the group shares
Venn diagrams with hoops and toys
Categories in everyday life: animals, foods, tools
Finding more than one sensible way to sort
projects: A family sorting game the child invents and teaches at home
week_5_6.practice: Picture sorting puzzles of our own design

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Analogies and Relationships
topics: A is to B as C is to what: relationships with pictures
Relationships of size, part and whole, and before and after
Shape analogies: what change turned the first shape into the second
Number relationships: one more, double, half
Saying the relationship before choosing the answer
Checking that the same change works both times
projects: Draw three picture analogies of your own for the class to solve
week_7_8.practice: Original picture and shape analogy cards
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 puzzle check: patterns, sorting and analogies, explained aloud

phase_2_spatial_and_quantitative.title: PHASE 2: Spatial and Quantitative Reasoning (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_spatial_and_quantitative.description: Thinking with shapes in space, and thinking with numbers, both built on hands-on play before pictures.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Rotations, Reflections and Shape Puzzles
topics: Turning a shape a quarter turn and a half turn
Mirror images and lines of symmetry
Tangram and pattern block puzzles
Building a shape from smaller shapes
Seeing a shape from a different side
Grids with shapes that follow a rule across and down
projects: A tangram picture book: five pictures built and named by the child
week_9_10.practice: Daily spatial play with blocks or paper shapes

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Folding, Cutting and Picturing
topics: Folding paper and predicting the shape when it opens
Cutting a folded paper and predicting the holes
Nets of cubes: which ones fold into a box
Counting cubes in a stack, including the hidden ones
Mazes and paths on a grid
Drawing what you picture before checking with real paper
projects: A folding and cutting predictions journal, checked with real paper each time
week_11_12.practice: Fold-and-cut challenges at home with scrap paper
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 puzzle check: spatial puzzles of our own, with real paper allowed for checking

month_4_quantitative.title: Month 4: Number Sense and Quantitative Reasoning

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Number Sense That Runs Deep
topics: Place value with tens and ones (and hundreds for ages 8 to 9)
Number bonds to 10 and 20 known by heart
Comparing and ordering numbers, and estimating amounts
Odd and even numbers and skip counting
Addition and subtraction strategies, not just answers
Early multiplication as equal groups (ages 8 to 9)
projects: A number-line wall chart the child builds and uses in class
week_13_14.practice: Number games at home: dice, cards and quick mental questions

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Balances, Number Series and Number Puzzles
topics: Balance puzzles: what makes both sides equal
Missing-number sentences, such as 9 equals 5 plus something
Number series that go up or down by a rule
Number series with two steps, such as add 2 then add 3
Comparing two groups of objects and making them equal
Explaining a number rule in words and testing it
projects: Invent a number series puzzle and a balance puzzle for the class
week_15_16.practice: Original number puzzle cards from easy to stretching
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 puzzle check: spatial and number puzzles, explained aloud

phase_3_putting_it_together.title: PHASE 3: Putting It Together (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_putting_it_together.description: Harder mixed puzzles, explaining thinking clearly, and a calm, honest look at what a group screening feels like.

month_5_mixed_reasoning.title: Month 5: Multi-Step Puzzles and Explaining Your Thinking

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Puzzles With Two Rules
topics: Shape grids where color and position both change
Number patterns hidden in shape puzzles
Classifying by two features at once
Logic puzzles: who has which pet, with simple clues
Trying an idea, checking it and trying again
Talking about a mistake as useful information
projects: A two-rule puzzle the child designs, with a written or spoken explanation
week_17_18.practice: Mixed original puzzles at home, a few minutes a day

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Listening, Choosing and Checking
topics: Listening carefully to a direction read aloud before starting
Looking at every option before choosing
Crossing out options that cannot be right
Working quietly on your own for a short set time
Staying calm when a puzzle feels hard
Picture-based thinking without needing to read
projects: A puzzle trail around the home with clues the child follows
week_19_20.practice: Short timed puzzle rounds of our own, kept light and fun
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 puzzle check: a mixed set of original puzzles in a quiet, timed round

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: What a Group Screening Is Like
topics: What happens on a screening day in general terms: a quiet room, a teacher reading directions and picture choices
Practising the format with our own original puzzles, never real or imitation test items
Taking turns, raising a hand and following instructions in a group
Short breaks, a good night's sleep and arriving rested
For parents: what CogAT, NNAT and OLSAT publishers say their tests measure
For parents: checking your own school's or district's process, which varies widely
projects: A calm-day plan made with the child, in pictures
week_21_22.practice: Light puzzle play only, to keep the fun

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Puzzle Portfolio and Next Steps
topics: Choosing favorite puzzles from the six months
Explaining a favorite puzzle to family in a short show-and-tell
Next steps in math: elementary math, olympiad-style puzzles or early coding
Keeping reasoning play going at home
Celebrating effort and curiosity, whatever any test says
A short note to parents on each child's strengths
projects: A puzzle portfolio: the child's own invented puzzles from the course
week_23_24.practice: A take-home puzzle pack of our own for the holidays
week_23_24.assessment: Final check: the puzzle portfolio and a friendly talk-through with the teacher

faqs.question: Is this a CogAT or NNAT test prep course?
faqs.answer: Not in the drilling sense. It is a reasoning class that builds the broad skills these tests aim to measure: patterns, spatial thinking, classifying and number sense. Near the end, children see the general format of a group screening so the day feels familiar. Every puzzle is our own, and none is presented as a real test item.

faqs.question: What does the CogAT measure?
faqs.answer: Riverside Insights, its publisher, says the CogAT "shows us how well a child can reason abstractly and identify patterns and relationships in the world around them", unlike an achievement test. It has Verbal, Quantitative and Nonverbal batteries, and at the levels for grades K to 2 the items are picture based.

faqs.question: What are the NNAT and OLSAT?
faqs.answer: Both are published by Pearson. Pearson describes the NNAT3 as "a nonverbal measure of general ability for students in kindergarten through grade 12", and says the OLSAT 8 "assesses verbal, nonverbal, and quantitative cognitive abilities for K-12 students". Which test, if any, your child takes depends on your school or district.

faqs.question: Should children prepare for these tests at all?
faqs.answer: Some districts say no specific study is needed. Seattle Public Schools says of the NGAT it gives first graders: "The NGAT is not designed to measure skills that can be learned through studying or test preparation." We agree that drilling is the wrong idea. What helps is broad reasoning play, strong number sense and simply knowing what a quiet group test feels like, which is what this course offers.

faqs.question: Does NYC use a test for Gifted and Talented?
faqs.answer: The process NYC Public Schools describes for fall 2027 entry includes no test. Kindergarten eligibility comes from pre-K teacher nominations or Division of Early Childhood Education interviews, and for grades 1 to 4 eligibility is based on report card grades of 3 or 4 in Math, Reading and Writing. This course still helps a curious child enjoy and explain their thinking.

faqs.question: What age is right?
faqs.answer: The course is for ages 6 to 9, taught in two bands: ages 6 to 7 and ages 8 to 9. The younger band uses more objects and pictures; the older band adds harder number reasoning and two-rule puzzles. The free demo class helps us place each child.

faqs.question: My child cannot read well yet. Can they join?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most puzzles are pictures, shapes and numbers, and the teacher reads every direction aloud. Reasoning without reading is exactly what much of the course practices.

faqs.question: Can you guarantee a place in a gifted program?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody honest can. Each district sets its own process, and many use more than one measure. We promise lively, thoughtful classes and real growth in reasoning, and a short note on each child's strengths at the end.

faqs.question: We live in the UK. Is this useful?
faqs.answer: Yes, as enrichment. UK schools notice more able children in different ways, and this course gives a curious child more patterns, spatial puzzles and number reasoning than a typical classroom has time for. It runs live online, so families join from anywhere.

faqs.question: Are you connected with Riverside Insights, Pearson or any school district?
faqs.answer: No. We are an independent online school and are not connected with or endorsed by Riverside Insights, Pearson, NYC Public Schools, Seattle Public Schools or any district. CogAT, NNAT and OLSAT are trademarks of their owners. Always check your own school's or district's process.

faqs.question: How are the classes run, and can we try one?
faqs.answer: Short live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group batch of 15 to 20 children or 1-on-1. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays. The first class is free, with no obligation to enrol.
